42858215.label: Purpose
42858215.text: To assess if PSA density (PSAD) velocity is a predictor of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa).

42858215.label: Methods
42858215.text: Patients undergoing prostate MR for suspected csPCa between 2017 and 2023 were included. Of these, patients who underwent two or more MR exams within 0.3 to 2 years to each other and pathological confirmation within 1 year after the last MR were identified. PI-RADS score, patient age, no-prior-PCa cohort or active surveillance (AS), PSA, PSAD, PSA-velocity and PSAD-velocity were assessed if they were predictor of csPCa. For univariate analysis, all variables were assessed using student t or chi-square tests. When variables were considered significant, variables were entered into multivariate logistic regression model. To assess whether PSAD-velocity adds diagnostic value beyond established predictors, we compared a base model (age, PI-RADS score, clinical cohort, and current PSAD) with the same model plus PSAD-velocity, using optimism-corrected AUC from 1,000 bootstrap resamples.

42858215.label: Results
42858215.text: 23,244 MRs were performed (17,703 for no-prior-PCa, 5,541 for AS). 1,174 patients (mean age: 65.9 years) met the inclusion criteria, and 550 (46.8%) were diagnosed with csPCa. On univariate analysis, PI-RADS score (p<.0001), age (67.0 vs. 64.9 years, p<.0001), AS status (67% vs. 59%, p = .004), PSA (7.5 vs. 6.6 ng/mL, p<.001), PSAD (p<.0001), and PSAD-velocity (0.023 vs. 0.012 ng/mL/mL/year, p = .005) were associated with csPCa, but PSA-velocity (1.4 vs. 1.2 ng/mL/year, p=.38) was not. On multivariable analysis, PI-RADS score (p<.0001), age (p<.0001), AS status (p = .002), PSA (p<.0001), and PSAD (p<.0001) remained significant predictors, but PSAD-velocity was not (p = .13). Adding PSAD-velocity to the base model produced no significant improvement in optimism-corrected AUC (0.7605 vs. 0.7611; ΔAUC = + 0.0006, 95% CI -0.0002 to +0.0019).

42858215.label: Conclusions
42858215.text: Higher PSAD-velocity was associated with presence of csPCa on univariate analysis but not on multivariate analysis, and on fixed-model analysis did not meaningfully improve diagnostic discrimination beyond established predictors.

42880965.text: Large language models show great promise for clinical decision support but generally lack medical imaging integration. Therefore, vision-language models have been proposed, but there is little evidence on their performance, particularly compared with conventional machine learning. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is a well-established treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but it is still not known which patients will be good long-term responders. Therefore, this study proposes a physician-inspired visual question answering (VQA) framework that emulates the structured integration of PSMA-directed imaging and clinical data used in routine clinical assessment for overall survival prognostication. Methods: As a proof of concept, we conducted a retrospective, multicenter study across 2 academic institutions that included 110 patients with mCRPC who were treated with either [177Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T or [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Our VQA approach incorporates a 3-dimensional image encoder, the domain-specific language model RadBERT, and a cross-modal transformer to process baseline and interim (after 2 cycles) PET and SPECT images, clinical data, and clinical query. The model was trained to predict 24-mo survival, and performance was compared with state-of-the-art approaches. External validation was performed with the [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 cohort. Results: The VQA model outperformed all state-of-the-art approaches while showing accuracy comparable to the query-free attention multimodal fusion model. Specifically, it achieved 81.8% accuracy (95% CI, 0.52-0.95) when integrating SPECT or PET images with prostate-specific antigen measurements. External validation of the VQA showed 71.9% accuracy (95% CI, 0.53-0.86) after few-shot fine-tuning, with further improvement over all state-of-the-art approaches in survival stratification. The VQA approach showed the closest calibration with the ground-truth survival distribution, with no significant differences observed (log-rank test, P = 0.76). Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed the highest area under the curve (0.75) among the evaluated models. Together, these findings suggest that the VQA approach demonstrated adaptability across different PSMA ligands while maintaining slightly improved yet comparable overall survival prognostic performance. Conclusion: By adopting a physician-inspired assessment workflow, the VQA framework shows advantages in integrating imaging and laboratory data for clinical decision support compared with conventional machine learning. The preliminary results indicate that VQA-based approaches warrant future evaluation for survival prognostication in patients with mCRPC who are receiving PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

42913765.text: The International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) established 26 consensus quality indicators (QIs) for lung cancer screening (LCS) programs, of which 20 were rated as essential and 6 as desirable by the expert panel. We evaluated the extent to which the American College of Radiology (ACR) Lung Cancer Screening Registry (LCSR), the largest LCS registry in the U.S., can support measurement of the IASLC QIs. We performed a crosswalk analysis, mapping all 26 IASLC QIs to the LCSR Data Dictionary and its 46 clinical performance measures, classifying each as directly measurable, derivable, or not measurable. The crosswalk was reviewed and independently validated by members of the ACR Early Lung Cancer Detection Registry Quality and Education Committee. Eight QIs (30.8%) were directly measurable, 10 (38.5%) were derivable, and 8 (30.8%) were not measurable from LCSR data alone. The LCSR therefore contains sufficient data elements to support measurement of approximately 69% of IASLC QIs. Remaining gaps involve screening uptake, clinical investigation, procedure complications, curative-intent treatment, treatment equity, diagnostic investigation equity and selected wait-time measures and would require additional registry fields or external data linkage.

42951765.label: Background
42951765.text: Increased epicardial adipose tissue volume (EATV) is a risk marker for future myocardial infarction (MI), but its value beyond SCORE2 (Systemic Coronary Risk Evaluation 2), the coronary artery calcium score (CACS) and the coronary artery segment involvement score (SIS) remains poorly studied.

42951765.label: Objectives
42951765.text: To determine the incremental value of EATV normalized to heart volume (EATVh) on top of SCORE2, CACS and SIS in predicting future MI.

42951765.label: Methods
42951765.text: We studied associations between EATVh, SCORE2, CACS, SIS and the risk of MI in a general population cohort of 25,155 participants (age 50-64, 50.7% women). Sex-stratified multivariable Cox-regression estimated hazard ratios (HR) and ROC-analysis with variables dichotomized at their 75th percentile assessed incremental predictive value.

42951765.label: Results
42951765.text: A total of 304 MI (71 in women) occurred during follow-up (median: 7.8 years). In adjusted analysis, EATVh and SCORE2 were independently associated with MI in women, but only SIS and SCORE2 in men. The highest HR per EATVh IQR was found in women <55 years (1.89). ROC-analysis showed that adding EATVh to SCORE2, CACS and SIS improved MI prediction in women but not men (AUC: 0.681 vs. 0.667; p < 0.05 for both).

42951765.label: Conclusions
42951765.text: EATVh provides independent, modest incremental information on the risk of future MI in women on top of CACS and SIS, but not in men. Further studies in more diverse population segments including younger and symptomatic individuals are warranted.

42982615.text: Cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) continues to expand, creating a parallel need to develop the clinicians, educators, investigators, and leaders who will advance the field. This opinion paper frames mentorship and sponsorship as essential professional infrastructure rather than episodic networking. Using the Fellow and Resident Leaders of the Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography (FiRST) Committee and the SCCT Future Leaders Program (FLP) as complementary models, we describe five interconnected domains: connection, education, scholarship, visibility, and leadership. Activities include speed mentoring, educational resource development, mentored writing, scientific communication, and Society service. A retrospective descriptive evaluation of 73 FiRST alumni and 15 FLP alumni who completed participation by December 31, 2025 documented subsequent SCCT committee service in 43.8% and 80.0%, committee chair or vice-chair roles in 16.4% and 20.0%, and Board membership in 9.6% and 13.3%, respectively. Median publication counts were 48 (interquartile range [IQR], 18-131) for FiRST and 57 (IQR, 45-78.5) for FLP; median h-indices were 13 (IQR, 6-28) and 13 (IQR, 10.5-19). These findings describe recorded career achievements and cumulative scholarship, not effects attributable to program participation. We propose prospective evaluation of mentorship continuity, scholarly contributions, leadership, retention, and barriers to participation. Intentional investment in mentorship, sponsorship, and inclusive opportunities can help professional societies connect early engagement with sustained contribution and prepare the future CCT workforce.

42988565.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, with a 5-y survival rate of approximately 20%. Although glypican-3-targeted radiotheranostics are under development, a plurality of patients with HCC lack glypican-3 expression, underscoring the need for alternative targetable antigens. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is overexpressed in 50%-70% of HCC tumors and represents a clinically validated therapeutic target. Here, we developed and evaluated a panitumumab-based EGFR-targeted radiotheranostic pair, [89Zr]Zr-desferrioxamine-panitumumab ([89Zr]Zr-Pani) for immuno-PET and [225Ac]Ac-Macropa-panitumumab ([225Ac]Ac-Pani) for targeted α-particle therapy, in clinically relevant orthotopic HCC models. Methods: Panitumumab was conjugated with desferrioxamine or Macropa chelators and radiolabeled with 89Zr or 225Ac, respectively. EGFR expression was characterized across a panel of HCC cell lines. Binding affinity, biodistribution, and tumor specificity were assessed in subcutaneous and orthotopic Huh-7 models, with EGFR-mediated targeting confirmed by blocking (200-fold molar excess of unlabeled panitumumab). Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in mice bearing orthotopic Huh-7-Luc+ tumors (n = 6 per group) after a single 9.3 kBq dose of [225Ac]Ac-Pani, with longitudinal monitoring by bioluminescence imaging, [89Zr]Zr-Pani immuno-PET, and blood chemistry. Results: [89Zr]Zr-Pani exhibited high-affinity binding to EGFR (dissociation constant, 0.35 nM) and demonstrated robust tumor accumulation in both subcutaneous Huh-7 (20.6 ± 2.6 %IA/g) and orthotopic Huh-7-Luc+ tumors (19.3 ± 2.0 %IA/g) at 120-192 h postinjection. Biodistribution of [225Ac]Ac-Pani closely mirrored that of [89Zr]Zr-Pani across organs and tumors, with tumor uptake reduced approximately 5-fold by blocking (21.7 ± 1.1 vs. 4.5 ± 0.6 %IA/g; P < 0.0001), confirming EGFR-specific targeting. A single 9.3 kBq administration of [225Ac]Ac-Pani induced substantial early tumor regression and significantly prolonged median survival (70 d) compared with vehicle (28 d) and blocking (35 d) groups (log-rank P < 0.0001), with no clinically meaningful hepatotoxicity or renal toxicity. However, tumor regrowth eventually occurred in all treated mice. Conclusion: [89Zr]Zr-Pani and [225Ac]Ac-Pani represent a radiotheranostic pair that enables EGFR-specific imaging and targeted α-particle therapy in orthotopic HCC models. These findings establish EGFR as a promising radiotheranostic target in HCC, broadening the patient population eligible for image-guided radiopharmaceutical interventions for liver cancer.

43002565.text: For active surveillance assessment, 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT was performed in a 73-year-old man with Gleason 3+3 prostate adenocarcinoma. PET/CT showed a markedly enlarged prostate indenting the bladder base, with focal midline activity suggestive of prostatic urethral urinary retention. Intravenous furosemide was administered before 120-minute delayed imaging, which showed complete resolution of the activity and excluded pathologic uptake. After discharge, he developed urinary urgency and incomplete emptying, progressing to lower abdominal and pelvic pain with elevated creatinine. Postrenal acute kidney injury from acute urinary retention was diagnosed. Catheterization and inpatient monitoring normalized renal function, highlighting an underrecognized risk of forced diuresis.

43019565.text: A 62-year-old man had dizziness and dysarthria for 4 months and limited mobility of the left upper extremity for 1 month. An outside enhanced MR showed a space-occupying lesion in the right frontal lobe. Since the patient had pancreaticoduodenectomy, gastrostomy, and jejunostomy 8.5 years ago for poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the small intestine, brain metastasis was suspected. FDG PET/CT demonstrated increased FDG activity in the right frontal lobe lesion, but no FDG-avid lesion was found in other parts of the body. Following surgical resection, histopathology examination indicated sarcoma. The patient underwent brain radiotherapy afterward.

43020615.text: The Highlights Lecture, presented at the closing session of each SNMMI Annual Meeting, was originated and presented for more than 30 y by Henry N. Wagner, Jr., MD. Beginning in 2010, the duties of summarizing selected significant presentations at the meeting were divided annually among 4 distinguished nuclear and molecular medicine subject matter experts. The 2026 Highlights Lectures were delivered on June 2, 2026 at the SNMMI Annual Meeting in Los Angeles, California. Presented here is the lecture by David M. Schuster, MD, FACR, Emory University Hospital in Atlanta, Georgia, who spoke on oncology and therapy topics presented at the meeting. Note that in the following presentation summary, numerals in brackets represent abstract numbers as published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine (2026;67[suppl 1]).

43021015.label: Objectives
43021015.text: To assess the reproducibility of a segmental functional liver imaging score (S-FLIS) and whether it improves risk stratification in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) beyond global FLIS (G-FLIS) and established MRI/MRCP-based scores (ANALI, ANALI Gd+, DiStrict), alone or combined.

43021015.label: Materials and methods
43021015.text: This prospective study included consecutive adult PSC patients undergoing standardised gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI, blood tests and liver stiffness measurement (LSM). G-FLIS, S-FLIS, DiStrict, ANALI and ANALI Gd+ were computed, and interobserver agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa. Univariate and bivariate logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses evaluated discrimination for two surrogate risk biomarkers: LSM > 9.6 kPa and Mayo risk score (MRS) > 0.

43021015.label: Results
43021015.text: Seventy-seven patients were included (median age 45 years; 62.3% male). Interobserver agreement was almost perfect for DiStrict (κ = 0.98), substantial for G-FLIS (κ = 0.608) and moderate to almost perfect for S-FLIS across hepatic segments (κ = 0.524-0.861). Unlike G-FLIS, S-FLIS was significantly associated with both high LSM and high MRS. Among individual scores, S-FLIS achieved the highest discriminative performance for high LSM (AUC = 0.782) and high MRS (AUC = 0.816), outperforming ANALI (0.668 and 0.702) and DiStrict (0.713 and 0.741). Bivariate models combining ANALI and S-FLIS achieved the highest performance for both endpoints (AUC = 0.843 and 0.864).

43021015.label: Conclusion
43021015.text: S-FLIS outperformed established morphological MRI/MRCP scores in identifying high-risk PSC patients, and pairing functional (S-FLIS) with morphological (ANALI) assessment yielded the greatest incremental value, supporting a multiparametric non-invasive approach to risk stratification in PSC.

43021015.label: Key points
43021015.text: Question Can an S-FLIS improve non-invasive risk stratification in PSC beyond whole-liver FLIS and established morphological MRI/MRCP scores, alone or in combination? Findings S-FLIS outperformed FLIS, ANALI, and DiStrict as a standalone discriminator of high-risk PSC patients, and its combination with ANALI achieved the highest discriminative accuracy (AUC up to 0.864). Clinical relevance S-FLIS is a reproducible, non-invasive MRI biomarker of hepatocellular function in PSC; combined with the morphological ANALI score, it may enhance non-invasive risk stratification, pending validation in larger multicenter cohorts.

43064865.label: Objectives
43064865.text: The molar tooth sign (MTS) is based on maloriented superior cerebellar peduncles (SCPs), a deepened interpeduncular fossa, and vermian hypoplasia, which may be less clearly delineable prenatally. Phenotypic assessment of patients with suspected Joubert syndrome (JS) was conducted, and additional morphological characteristics of JS on fetal MRI were defined.

43064865.label: Materials and methods
43064865.text: In this retrospective study, phenotypic assessment was performed for patients with a fetal MRI-based suspected diagnosis of JS. Analysis of the fetal brain included detection of MTS, brainstem anomalies, elevation of the fastigium in the midsagittal plane, thickened SCP with a course parallel to the anterior/middle cerebral fossa in the parasagittal plane, cerebellar dysplasia, cephaloceles, and extracerebral ciliopathic manifestations.

43064865.label: Results
43064865.text: Eleven patients were identified and analyzed-three cases with genetic confirmation of JS, three with incomplete genetic testing, five without confirmatory genetic testing. Classical MTS was present in 55% of cases. Pathological appearance of the SCPs was observed in 73%, and dysplastic cerebellum and brainstem hypo- or dysplasia in 100%. Elevation of the fastigium was observed in 91%, cephaloceles in 46%, and extracerebral anomalies, especially renal, in 64%. All cases showed a hypo- and dysplastic vermis.

43064865.label: Conclusion
43064865.text: This study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and accompanying anomalies commonly observed in patients with a suspected diagnosis of JS. JS can be suspected on fetal MRI even in the absence of classical MTS based on characteristic anomalies of the SCPs, brainstem, and cerebellum in combination with extracerebral anomalies supporting this diagnosis.

43064865.label: Key points
43064865.text: QuestionWhat are phenotypical presentations of patients with suspected Joubert syndrome (JS) in fetal MRI and can JS be suspected in absence of molar tooth sign? FindingsJS can be suspected in fetal MRI without MTS based on characteristic changes in superior cerebellar peduncles, brainstem, and cerebellum and co-occurring extracerebral anomalies. Clinical relevanceThis exploratory study provides novel insights into the prenatal presentation of molar tooth malformations and associated anomalies commonly observed in cases with suspected JS. These findings may aid counseling physicians in selecting appropriate pregnancy management for patients with suspected JS.
